title: Recursion Schemes
body:
[[Recursion]] already owns *what recursion is*: base case, recursive case, and the
[[Stack and Heap|stack frame]] each call costs. This note owns the thing that changes when you
take the loop away: recursion stops being a technique you reach for occasionally and becomes
**the only means of repetition there is**, so its recurring *shapes* are worth naming.

In [[C]] you would write a loop and use recursion for trees. In [[Haskell]] there is no loop,
so every traversal, every accumulation, and every search is one of the four patterns below.

## The four shapes

### Structural recursion

Recurse on the structure of the argument, one constructor at a time. A list is either `[]` or
`x : xs`, so a function over lists has exactly two equations:

```haskell
length' :: [a] -> Int
length' []       = 0
length' (_ : xs) = 1 + length' xs
```

This is the default and it is the one that matters most, because **it is guaranteed to
terminate**: the argument is strictly smaller at every step and `[]` is reachable from any
finite list. That guarantee is what makes structural induction a valid proof technique over
exactly the same shape, which is the whole of [[Program Correctness]].

### Accumulator passing

Carry the answer-so-far in an extra parameter instead of building it on the way back up:

```haskell
reverse' :: [a] -> [a]
reverse' xs = go xs []
  where go []       acc = acc
        go (y : ys) acc = go ys (y : acc)
```

The naive `reverse (x:xs) = reverse xs ++ [x]` is $O(n^2)$, because `++` walks its left
argument every time. The accumulator version is $O(n)$. Same answer, different cost, and
noticing which one you have written is most of the practical skill.

### Tail recursion

A call is **tail recursive** when the recursive call is the last thing the function does, with
no work left to do on its result. `go` above is tail recursive; `length'` is not, because it
still has to add 1.

The reason it matters is the one [[Recursion]] gives: each pending call holds a
[[Stack and Heap|stack frame]]. A tail call has nothing pending, so the compiler can reuse the
frame rather than pushing a new one, turning the recursion into a jump. That is exactly the
loop the language does not have, recovered by the compiler. In [[Assembly]] terms it is a `bra`
where a `jsr` would have been; see [[Subroutines]].

Haskell complicates this: because of [[Lazy Evaluation]], an accumulator can build a chain of
unevaluated thunks instead of a value, so a "tail recursive" sum can still exhaust memory. The
fix is to force the accumulator (`seq`, or a strict fold).

### Mutual and tree recursion

Two functions calling each other (`even'`/`odd'`), or one function calling itself twice, as any
walk over a [[Tree]] does. Tree recursion is where the shape genuinely cannot be a loop
without an explicit [[Stack]], which is the point [[Depth First Search]] makes from the other
direction.

## Folds are these patterns with a name

`foldr` and `foldl` abstract the first two shapes so you stop rewriting them:

```haskell
sum'     = foldr (+) 0
length'' = foldr (\_ n -> n + 1) 0
reverse''= foldl (flip (:)) []
```

`foldr` is structural recursion, `foldl` is accumulator passing. Almost every list function in
the language is one of the two with a different operator handed in, which is
[[Partial Application]] doing the work.

## Core Facts to Know

- With no loop, recursion is the only repetition; see [[Haskell]].
- **Structural** recursion follows the data's constructors and always terminates on finite data.
- That termination guarantee is what licenses structural induction in [[Program Correctness]].
- An **accumulator** carries the result down instead of building it on the way back up.
- Naive `reverse` is $O(n^2)$; the accumulator version is $O(n)$.
- **Tail recursion**: the recursive call is the last action, so the frame can be reused.
- Tail-call optimisation turns recursion into a jump, recovering the loop.
- Laziness can defeat it: an unforced accumulator builds thunks instead of a value.
- `foldr` is structural recursion; `foldl` is accumulator passing.
